column2: The Burden of the Italian Peace
The defeated ministry faces indemnities, inquiries into the campaign and a shaken officer corps. The treaty burdens public credit while the army restores its confidence.
The Army of the National Settlement
The successful campaign has strengthened the confidence of soldiers and officers in the national command.
The Reckoning after the French War
Parliament, the cabinet and the army must reckon with a failed national adventure. Indemnities and military inquiries hamper the work of recovery.
The Prestige of the French Army
Victory across the Alps restores confidence in the command and strengthens the ministry's authority abroad.
The Paris Border Guarantees
Italy has accepted limits upon frontier military establishments as part of a negotiated territorial settlement. The concession falls upon the national military budget.

The Italian Claim to Savoy and Nice

The Italian ambassador has laid his government's claim before the ministry. Ministers who favour accommodation argue that an agreed frontier could remove a lasting cause of hostility. Their opponents warn that yielding French soil would expose the government to accusations of weakness. A convention might reconcile the cabinets through guarantees limiting Italian military preparations along the new frontier. Paris must decide whether to accept the territorial articles, open that negotiation, or reject the demand and face the prospect of war.
Authorise the draft and seek French ratification.
Reject the conditions and prepare for war.
A Convention Offered by Paris

Paris is willing to discuss the cession, but its ministers ask that Italy limit military preparations on the new frontier. The general staff dislikes a promise that constrains its establishments, while the foreign ministry believes a peaceful recovery of the disputed provinces worth the concession. The convention still requires French ratification. Acceptance here authorises our ambassador to sign the draft, it does not place the provinces under Italian administration before Paris has confirmed the instrument.
Ratify the convention.
Withhold ratification.
Ratification of the Italian Convention

The Italian government has accepted the draft frontier guarantees. Our ambassador recommends ratification before opponents of the convention can harden opinion on either side of the Alps. Ministers may nevertheless decide that the agreement gives away too much. A second refusal would end the negotiation: the Italian cabinet has warned that it will seek a wider settlement by force, and Corsica as well as the Alpine frontier would then become an object of the war.
Enforce the national settlement when our treaties permit.
The French Negotiations Have Broken Down

The ambassador reports that no convention can be concluded. The Italian cabinet has resolved to seek a national settlement by arms, extending its demands to the French possessions in Savoy, Nice and Corsica. The general staff is instructed to prepare the campaign. Existing alliances, a truce, foreign protection or a war already in progress may delay the declaration, in that case the unresolved ultimatum remains before the government until it can be enforced. A French victory would expose Italian territory to a counter-settlement.
Enforce the Rejected Claim to Savoy and Nice

The French refusal has left the national ultimatum unresolved. Issue the declaration once peace and treaty obligations permit it. Our war articles seek the French possessions in Savoy, Nice and Corsica, defeat would expose Italy to a French counter-settlement.
Require an answer from Paris.
The Ambassador Renews the French Mission

The foreign ministry has found an unanswered territorial mission in its correspondence. The ambassador is instructed to place the proposal before the French cabinet and obtain a formal answer. The original appropriation remains the authority for the mission, no fresh levy is required.
Place the ultimatum before the cabinet.
The Unresolved French Ultimatum

A previous refusal has not been followed by a settlement. Ministers place the outstanding ultimatum before the cabinet, with the military preparations and treaty obligations that must govern its enforcement.
Await the French cabinet's answer.

The Peace Conference with France

The French government has accepted the Italian war articles. Delegates must now draw the frontier and arrange the occupation of the ceded districts. Savoy and Nice will pass with Corsica into the Italian state, while French indemnities meet part of the expense of the campaign. The ministry in Paris faces the burden of defeat and its army must rebuild confidence. Our officers return with enhanced authority, but ministers caution that victory does not settle every grievance along the Alpine frontier. Provincial officials are to preserve ordinary administration during the transfer.
Secure the Aosta valley.
Demand Sardinia for our naval position.
Demand the valley and Sardinia.
Accept indemnities and the public humiliation.
The French Conference after the Italian War

Italy has failed to enforce its ultimatum and has accepted the French counter-articles. The ministry may demand a strategic frontier in the Aosta valley, naval positions in Sardinia, or the combination of both. A more restrained party would retain the indemnities and public humiliation while leaving the Italian frontier intact. Officers insist that a visible settlement must justify the campaign, diplomats warn that a sweeping territorial punishment could make the next Italian war more likely. The defeated Italian government will bear the temporary fiscal and military consequences whatever frontier is chosen.
Record the French settlement and begin recovery.
The French Terms of Peace

The French delegates have published the counter-settlement. Provincial officials must obey the frontier articles, while the treasury meets the indemnities and the army answers for the failed campaign. The cabinet cannot repair the defeat by another proclamation. Ministers must restore public credit, rebuild military confidence and decide whether a future policy can reconcile the country with the peace.
Prepare a diplomatic dossier for the Alpine frontier.
Claims and the Concert of Europe

The proclamation of national claims has reached our embassies. It cannot by itself transfer a district governed by another crown. The Alpine frontier poses a question of language, security and the rights of inhabitants who do not all share the same national allegiance. Ministers propose that Britain or Germany be asked to mediate before the cabinet resorts to an ultimatum. A continental war would involve the alliances of both states, and the general staff cannot assume that the dispute would remain confined to the Alps.
An Italian Request for British Mediation

The Italian ambassador requests our good offices in a dispute with the Habsburg crown. Italy seeks a settlement in Trentino, South Tyrol and the Adriatic districts, where national claims overlap with the interests of several peoples. Accepting mediation commits us to transmit the proposal and hear the answer, it is no promise of military support. Our ministry may instead decline to take responsibility for an arrangement that could disturb the continental balance.

The Mediator Declines

Our ambassador has been informed that the requested mediation will not be undertaken. The refusal is not a judgment upon every Italian claim, but it deprives the ministry of an intermediary. The cabinet can now address the Habsburg government directly, accepting responsibility for the diplomatic exchange and any subsequent ultimatum.
Accept the full frontier convention.

The Italian Alpine Proposal

Italy has presented its frontier dossier. A sweeping acceptance would cede the districts named in the proposal, including the northern Tyrol, where language and allegiance make the Italian demand particularly contentious. Ministers favouring accommodation propose to surrender Trentino while retaining the northern districts and the Adriatic ports. Others regard even this concession as an invitation to further claims. The cabinet must weigh the national question against strategic communications, provincial loyalties and the danger of another continental conflict.
Accept Trentino and close the dossier.
Insist upon the full frontier settlement.
A Limited Alpine Convention

The Habsburg ministry offers Trentino while retaining South Tyrol and the Adriatic districts. Our diplomats consider the offer a tangible settlement obtained without war. National committees object that it abandons other claims, and officers fear that a narrow convention will leave the strategic dispute unresolved. Acceptance closes this diplomatic dossier and incorporates only the offered district, insistence on the full claim prepares the ground for a later ultimatum.
Keep the claim before the cabinet.
The Alpine Negotiations Fail

The exchange has produced no convention acceptable to both courts. Italian national committees demand action, but ministers must consider the army, public credit and the alliances surrounding the Habsburg crown. The outstanding claim may become an ultimatum when the government is ready. Such a declaration could draw allied powers into a wider conflict, neither mediation nor a national proclamation guarantees a short war.
Publish the convention and instruct the provincial authorities.
The Alpine Frontier Convention

The frontier convention has been signed. Surveyors and provincial officials will carry out the articles, while local courts and municipal offices continue their ordinary work during the transfer. The cabinet has obtained territory by agreement and must now show that national administration can respect the inhabitants whose language or allegiance differs from that of the cabinet.
Issue the Alpine Frontier Ultimatum

The diplomatic exchange has failed. Declare war for the full Alpine and Adriatic articles once the army and treaty obligations permit. Allied powers may enter on either side. The war settlement covers only the Habsburg government's possessions named in the dossier.

The Civil Charter of Libya

Annexation has placed Libya under the Italian government, but a change of sovereignty supplies no civil charter. Officers ask whether military government is to continue, magistrates need instructions concerning local law, municipal offices and property. Settlers and merchants press for institutions familiar to them, while the existing population expects its courts and communal rights to survive. Ministers propose national incorporation, a provincial compact, or a concession administration. Each course gives different authority to the crown and carries different burdens. None can turn the inhabitants into Italians merely by decree.
Libya is our Quarta Sponda, as Italian as Naples or Venice!
